data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: Cambodia is heavily dollarized and the National Bank of Cambodia manages a tightly managed float of the riel against the dollar, which has kept inflation low outside commodity shocks: it spiked to 25.0% in 2008 on food and fuel prices, then stayed in the 1-6% range for a decade, with 5.3% in 2022 and a projected 2.5% in 2025. Dollarization limits monetary transmission but also anchors expectations; the central bank's main tools are reserve management and macroprudential measures. The framework has worked, though it leaves Cambodia exposed to US monetary cycles.
debt_management: Public debt is low and stable, rising only from 26.6% of GDP in 2006 to a projected 26.5% in 2025, dipping to 21.2% in 2019 before COVID nudged it up. Borrowing is mostly concessional from bilateral and multilateral creditors, heavily China-linked for infrastructure. GDP grew from $8.4bn to a projected $49.3bn over the period, keeping ratios contained. The contingent risk is opaque liabilities around Chinese-financed projects and fast private credit growth rather than sovereign debt itself.

key_events.event: Commodity spike drove inflation to 25%; garment exports then slowed with the global crisis.
Post-election unrest and garment-sector strikes won minimum-wage increases.
EU partially withdrew EBA trade preferences over democratic backsliding; COVID hit tourism hard.
China-Cambodia free trade agreement took effect, deepening economic ties.
RCEP entered into force, boosting regional trade integration.
Hun Sen handed power to his son Hun Manet after elections the West deemed flawed.

outlook_next_decade: Cambodia should keep growing 5-6% on garments, tourism recovery, and manufacturing shifting from China, with debt staying manageable. Risks include loss of trade preferences if democratic conditions worsen, over-reliance on Chinese investment, real-estate and microfinance credit excesses, and climate vulnerability. Inflation is likely to stay low under the dollarized regime. The political succession's economic impact will depend on whether reform momentum continues.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
